Predict how the framework describes an innovation's effects first.

A ride-sharing app lets drivers earn flexible income and lets riders get around without owning a car, while also reducing the earnings of traditional taxi drivers in the same city. Which statement best characterizes the app's effects?
Correct. Some groups benefit (flexible drivers, carless riders) while another group is harmed (taxi drivers). A single innovation commonly produces both at once.
Incorrect. Ignoring the harm to taxi drivers tells only one side of the story.
Incorrect. Ignoring the benefits to riders and flexible drivers tells only one side of the story.
Incorrect. The app clearly changed how people earn and travel, so saying it has no effect is wrong.
Separate the original purpose from the surprise before matching an option.

Engineers create a smart thermostat intended to lower home energy bills. After it is widely adopted, a power company discovers it can use the aggregated data to predict neighborhood electricity demand and prevent blackouts. The blackout-prevention benefit is best described as:
Correct. The creators did not plan for demand prediction, so it is unintended, and it is clearly positive, so it is a beneficial unintended consequence.
Incorrect. The intended purpose was lowering home energy bills, not predicting demand across a neighborhood.
Incorrect. A program is integral to a smart thermostat, so it is a computing innovation.
Incorrect. Preventing blackouts is a benefit, not a harm, and nothing here says it outweighs anything.

I. A single effect of an innovation can be seen as beneficial by some people and harmful by others.

Incorrect. Statement III is also true, so 'I only' is too narrow.

After this lesson, you will be able to:
• Define the digital divide as unequal access to computing devices and to the Internet
• Identify factors that drive the divide, including income, geography, and demographics
• Explain how the divide affects who can participate in and benefit from computing
• Distinguish the local, national, and global levels at which the divide exists
• Describe evenhanded efforts that can reduce the divide, such as infrastructure, cost, and training

📈 Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 21 to 26 percent of the AP CSP exam, the single largest slice, and the digital divide is a favorite target because it is easy to write clear, fair questions about it. Nail the definition and the causes and you bank reliable points.
Two students are assigned the same online research project. One has a laptop at home and fast, reliable Internet
column2: the other shares a single phone with three siblings and can only get online at the public library before it closes. Both are equally smart and equally hardworking, yet one will almost certainly turn in more. What is actually different between them, and what would it take to close that gap?

column1: The digital divide is the unequal access to computing devices and to the Internet across different groups of people. That word, access, is the whole idea. The divide is not about who is smart or who is good with computers. It is about who has a working device, a reliable connection, and the ability to use them, and who does not.

Access is really two things at once. A person needs a device (a computer, tablet, or phone that can do the task) and a connection (Internet service that is fast and reliable enough to be useful). Having a phone but no home Internet, or having Internet so slow that a video call keeps dropping, still counts as being on the wrong side of the divide. The AP framework ties this directly to opportunity: access to computing shapes who can participate in and benefit from what computing offers.

When a question describes the digital divide, the key idea graders want is unequal access to computing and the Internet, and the resulting difference in who can participate. Answers that focus on access and opportunity beat answers about personal talent or interest almost every time.
The framework lists the groups the divide falls along. You should be able to recognize each factor:
Devices and monthly Internet service cost money. Lower-income households are less able to afford a good device or a fast plan.

Rural and remote areas often lack the infrastructure (cables, towers) that cities have, so service may be slow, expensive, or unavailable. This also differs between wealthier and less wealthy countries.
Access can differ by age, education level, and disability. For example, a site that is unusable with a screen reader shuts out some users regardless of their connection.
Even with a device and a connection, a person needs the skills to use them. Lack of training is its own barrier.

These factors overlap. A low-income household in a rural area faces both a cost barrier and an infrastructure barrier at the same time. The divide is also shaped by decisions, by governments, companies, and individuals, about where to build infrastructure, how to price service, and what to teach.

A town's homes are spread far apart in a remote area, and no company has run high-speed cable out to them, so residents can only get slow service at high prices. Which factor of the digital divide does this best illustrate?

So much of daily life now runs through computing: applying for jobs, doing schoolwork, seeing a doctor over video, filing government forms, banking, and finding information. When access is unequal, so is the chance to participate in and benefit from all of that. The divide can widen existing gaps, because the people who most need affordable services online are sometimes the least able to reach them.
The divide exists at three levels, and the exam expects you to tell them apart:
Local: differences between neighborhoods or households in the same town, such as which students have home Internet.
National: differences within one country, such as urban versus rural regions.
Global: differences between countries, where wealthier nations tend to have far higher access than lower-income ones.

The digital divide is about access and opportunity, not natural ability. A wrong answer will suggest some groups are simply ""not good with technology"" or ""not interested."" The framework is clear that the divide is a difference in access to devices, connection, and training, not a difference in how capable people are. If someone gets a device, a connection, and instruction, they can participate.
Because the divide comes from access barriers, efforts to reduce it target those barriers. The framework wants you to recognize the general categories, not to endorse any one plan:
Expanding infrastructure: building cable, fiber, or wireless coverage into areas that lack it.
Lowering cost: making devices and service more affordable, for example through subsidized plans or low-cost hardware.
Providing training: teaching digital literacy so people can actually use the access they gain.

These can come from governments, companies, nonprofits, schools, or individuals, and real solutions usually combine several. A program that ships free laptops but never provides Internet or instruction has only solved one piece of the problem. Keep your reasoning evenhanded: the exam asks which actions reduce access barriers, not which political approach is best.

A district gives every student a laptop but discovers many still cannot complete online homework because their homes have no Internet service. Which additional action would most directly reduce the remaining divide?
How 5.2 Is Tested on the Multiple-Choice Exam

Digital divide questions on the AP CSP exam cluster around three things, and knowing the shape of them makes the points easy. First, the definition: expect a question that asks what the digital divide is, where the correct answer names unequal access to computing devices and the Internet across groups. Second, the causes: a scenario will describe a person or community, and you identify which factor (income, geography, demographics, or digital literacy) explains their limited access, or which action would reduce that barrier. Third, the effects: questions connect access to who can participate in and benefit from computing, such as school, jobs, or services.

Two habits keep you out of the traps. Keep your framing evenhanded: the exam treats the divide as a matter of access and opportunity, never as a claim that some group is naturally worse with technology, and it does not favor one political solution over another. And read for level: notice whether a question is describing a local, national, or global gap, because the correct answer often hinges on that scope.

After this lesson, you will be able to:
• Explain that computing innovations can reflect existing human biases, usually unintentionally
• Identify the two main places bias enters a system: the data and the algorithm or design
• Explain why bias can exist even when no one intended it and can be hard to detect until use
• Locate the source of bias in a scenario as coming from the data or from the design
• Describe how programmers can reduce bias with representative data and testing with diverse users

📈 Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 5 to 8 percent of the AP CSP exam, and bias questions appear almost every year. They are quick concept points if you can tell where the bias entered and remember that bias does not require bad intent.

A company builds a resume-screening tool and trains it on ten years of its own past hiring decisions. The team writes careful, neutral code and never once tries to favor any group. A year later the tool is quietly ranking certain qualified applicants lower than others. Nobody wrote a rule to do that, so where did the bias actually come from, and how could a program end up biased when no one meant for it to be?

A computing innovation is anything that includes a program as an integral part, from a phone app to a machine-learning model. The AP CSP framework makes a claim you will be tested on: computing innovations can reflect existing human biases, sometimes on purpose but more often unintentionally. A program is built by people and trained on data produced by people, so any assumptions or imbalances baked into those people and that data can carry straight into the finished system.

The key word is unintentional. Bias in computing does not mean someone was malicious. Most biased systems are built by well-meaning teams who never wrote a single unfair rule. The bias slips in through the material they used and the choices they made about how the program should work, and it often stays invisible until real users start hitting it.

When a question describes a system that ends up treating some group unfairly, the strongest answer usually identifies where the bias entered (the data or the design) and notes that it can happen without anyone intending it. ""The programmers were dishonest"" is almost never the credited answer.
Two Places Bias Enters: Data and Algorithm
Bias can be embedded at two main points in a computing system, and the exam expects you to tell them apart.

Bias in the data happens when the information used to build or train the system does not fairly represent everyone it will affect. A face-recognition model trained mostly on photos of one group will work worse for the groups that were underrepresented in the photos.

Bias in the algorithm or design happens through the choices built into how the program works: which inputs it considers, what it ignores, and how heavily it weights each factor. If a loan model weights a factor that happens to track with one group, the design itself can produce a biased result even on balanced data.
The training or sample data is not representative of all users the system will affect.
An image classifier trained on photos of mostly one skin tone misidentifies people with other skin tones.
The choices about which inputs matter and how factors are weighted advantage or disadvantage some group.
A hiring model is designed to rank candidates by how closely they resemble past hires, so it keeps repeating the old pattern.
Sometimes both are present at once, but on the exam you should be ready to point to the primary source a scenario is describing.
A map app gives poor directions in rural areas because very few rural roads were included in the map information it was built from. This bias comes primarily from the:

Because bias usually arrives through imbalanced data or design choices rather than a deliberate rule, it can be present even when no one intended it, and it is often difficult to detect until the system is actually used by a wide range of people. A team testing only on users like themselves may see the program work perfectly and conclude it is fair, while a group they did not test with runs into failures. This is why real-world testing with diverse users matters so much: it surfaces bias that a small, similar test group would never reveal.

Bias in computing does NOT require bad intent. A very common wrong answer says a system can only be biased if its creators were prejudiced or trying to discriminate. The framework is explicit that bias is most often unintentional, entering through unrepresentative data or design choices. A team that meant well can still ship a biased system.
A team builds a photo tool and never intends to favor anyone, but it performs worse for some users. Which statement is correct?
The framework does not just describe bias, it expects designers to try to reduce it. Programmers and designers should take deliberate steps:
• Use representative data that reflects the full range of people the system will affect, not just the easiest group to collect.
Test with diverse users so failures that hurt a specific group show up before release, not after.
• Review the design to ask who could be disadvantaged by which inputs are used and how factors are weighted.

Bias can rarely be reduced to zero, and adding more data alone is not a guaranteed fix if that data is itself skewed. The point is that bias is something teams are responsible for looking for and reducing, not a fact of nature they can ignore.
How This Shows Up on the Exam

Topic 5.3 is tested almost entirely on the multiple-choice section, and the questions follow a small number of patterns. Most common is a short scenario in which a system produces an unfair or lopsided result, and you must identify the source of the bias: did it enter through the data (unrepresentative training or sample data) or through the algorithm and design (which inputs are used and how they are weighted)? A second frequent pattern checks whether you understand that bias can be unintentional, so answers that insist the creators must have been malicious are distractors, not the key. You may also see a question about reducing bias, where the credited answer involves representative data and testing with diverse users rather than simply removing a feature or adding more of the same skewed data. Read for who is affected and where the bias came from, and these become reliable points.

It can be. Working for a majority does not erase unfair results for a specific group. If the system consistently performs worse for one group because of its data or design, that is bias even if most users are served well.

After this lesson, you will be able to:
• Define crowdsourcing as obtaining input, ideas, content, labor, or funding from a large group of people
• Explain how the Internet and computing give crowdsourcing the reach, speed, and scale a small team cannot match
• Identify examples of crowdsourcing, including citizen science, crowdfunding, and collaborative content
• Describe the benefits and the quality and coordination concerns of crowdsourced work

📈 Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 21 to 26 percent of the AP CSP exam, the single largest slice. Crowdsourcing questions are fast, definition-driven points: if you can recognize the crowd, what it provides, and the role of the Internet in enabling it, you bank these reliably.

A museum has ten thousand old handwritten weather logs it wants turned into a searchable database, but its staff of three would need years to type them all in. Instead it posts scans online and asks the public to transcribe a page or two each. Within weeks the whole archive is done by strangers who never met. What made that possible, and what is this approach actually called?

Crowdsourcing is the practice of obtaining input, ideas, content, labor, or funding from a large group of people, often through the Internet, to accomplish a task or solve a problem. The key word is large. Instead of a small, fixed team doing all the work, a task is opened up to a big, often open crowd, and each contributor supplies a small piece. Add those pieces together and you get a result no small group could have produced as quickly, if at all.

The crowd can provide different things depending on the project. Sometimes it provides labor (people transcribing documents or classifying images), sometimes data (volunteers reporting bird sightings or road conditions), sometimes ideas or content (writing entries, submitting designs), and sometimes money (many small donations funding a project). Naming exactly what the crowd contributes is a favorite exam move.

When a scenario is crowdsourcing, the exam wants you to point to two things: a large group of people each contributing a small part, and the fact that the Internet or computing is what makes gathering those contributions at scale possible. If you can name both, you can answer almost any 5.4 question.
Crowdsourcing is an old idea, but the Internet transformed it. Computing gives a crowdsourced project three things a small team cannot match on its own:
Reach. A request posted online can be seen by millions of people across the world, so the potential pool of contributors is enormous.
Speed. Thousands of people can work in parallel at the same moment, so a task that would take one team years can finish in days.
Scale. Software collects, combines, and stores every small contribution automatically, so the size of the crowd is not limited by how much a coordinator can manually track.

Take those away and crowdsourcing shrinks back to whoever you can reach in person. That is why the framework ties crowdsourcing so tightly to computing: the Internet is not a minor detail of these examples, it is the enabling technology that gives the crowd its reach, speed, and scale.

A wildlife group asks people everywhere to photograph frogs in their area and upload the pictures with a location, building a nationwide map of where each species lives. What is the crowd primarily providing?
The exam expects you to recognize a few recurring flavors of crowdsourcing by their example, not by memorizing a definition word for word:
Data and labor: ordinary volunteers collect or classify observations
People worldwide count backyard birds or tag galaxies in telescope images so scientists can study far more data than a lab could gather alone.
Money: many small contributions add up to fund a project
An inventor raises money for a new gadget by collecting small pledges from thousands of online backers instead of one big investor.
Ideas and content: the public writes, edits, or reviews shared material
A public reference site where volunteers write and correct entries, or product ratings where many buyers each leave a review.
Notice they differ only in what the crowd supplies (data, money, or content) while sharing the same core: a large, open group each doing a little, gathered through the Internet.

Crowdsourcing is not just any group working together. A five-person class project or a company's normal design team is collaboration, but it is not crowdsourcing, because the group is small and closed. Crowdsourcing draws on a large, often open group, usually reached through the Internet. If the scenario has a small fixed team, it is collaboration, not crowdsourcing.

The upside of crowdsourcing is harnessing the knowledge, effort, or money of many people to do something no small team could. A crowd can label millions of images, spot a rare event happening somewhere in the world, or fund a project that no single backer would risk on.

But scale brings problems the exam also expects you to know. Quality and accuracy vary because contributions come from strangers with mixed expertise, so crowdsourced data or content usually needs verification. Coordination is hard when thousands of people work loosely on the same task. And attribution gets murky: when a crowd builds something together, deciding who gets credit or ownership is not obvious. Good crowdsourcing platforms design for these problems with review steps, guidelines, and reputation systems.

A startup's five employees meet each week to design their app together. A rival instead posts its design online and invites thousands of users worldwide to submit and vote on ideas. Which situation is crowdsourcing, and why?
How 5.4 Is Tested on the Multiple-Choice Exam

Crowdsourcing shows up in the multiple-choice section as short scenario questions, and there is no free-response component specific to this topic. Two skills earn the points. First, recognizing crowdsourcing: given a scenario, decide whether it counts, and the test is whether a large, often open group is each contributing a small piece, as opposed to a small fixed team (which is ordinary collaboration). Second, identifying what makes it possible: questions frequently ask why the approach works, and the intended answer is that the Internet and computing provide the reach, speed, and scale to gather many contributions that a small team could not. Expect distractors that describe small-group collaboration, or that credit better hardware or faster coding instead of the crowd and the network. Know the flavors (citizen science, crowdfunding, collaborative content) so you can name what the crowd supplies, and you will clear these quickly.

A charity used to raise money by mailing letters to a few hundred local residents. It now posts its campaign online, where anyone in the world can donate. Which best explains how computing changed what the charity can do?
Incorrect. Crowdsourcing does not guarantee larger individual donations. Its power is the number of contributors, not the size of each gift.

Four friends split the cost of a pizza and decide together which toppings to get. A student claims this is an example of crowdsourcing. Is the student correct?
Incorrect. Pooling money among four friends is not crowdfunding. The defining feature of crowdsourcing is a large, open group, not just more than one contributor.
Correct. Four friends are a small, closed group, so this is ordinary collaboration. Crowdsourcing requires a large, often open crowd, typically reached through the Internet.
Incorrect. Reaching a decision together is collaboration. Crowdsourcing specifically draws on a large, often open group, usually via the Internet.
Incorrect. Crowdsourcing can involve money (crowdfunding). The real reason this is not crowdsourcing is that the group is small and closed.

Judge each statement true or false before choosing.
I. Crowdsourcing can only be used to raise money, never to gather data or labor.
II. The Internet gives crowdsourcing reach, speed, and scale that a small team could not achieve alone.

Correct. II and III are both accurate: the Internet enables scale, and quality of mixed contributions is a real concern. I is false because crowdsourcing is not limited to money.
Incorrect. Statement I is false: crowdsourcing gathers data and labor too, not only money. So it cannot be part of the answer.
Incorrect. Statement I is false, so any choice that includes I is wrong, even though III is true.
Incorrect. Statement I is false, so all three cannot be correct.
Predict which flavor of crowdsourcing this is first.

An astronomy project posts millions of telescope images online and asks volunteers around the world to classify the shape of each galaxy, producing labeled data that researchers analyze. Which term best describes this activity?
Correct. Volunteers collecting or classifying scientific data at scale is citizen science, a form of crowdsourcing where the crowd supplies data and labor.
Incorrect. No money is being raised. Crowdfunding is crowdsourcing money, and this scenario gathers classifications, not funds.
Incorrect. Pair programming is two people sharing one computer to write code. It has nothing to do with a global crowd labeling images.
Incorrect. A single research team dividing work is small and closed. Here the labeling is done by a large, open crowd of volunteers online.
Predict the most likely downside before reading the options.

A travel site lets anyone post reviews and star ratings of hotels, and it shows the average rating for each hotel. Which of the following is the most significant concern a computer scientist would raise about this crowdsourced data?
Incorrect. Storage capacity is not the crowdsourcing concern here. Computing easily stores large numbers of reviews.
Incorrect. Averaging ratings is straightforward arithmetic. The real concern is the trustworthiness of the individual contributions.
Incorrect. The opposite is true: the Internet is exactly what lets the site reach a large audience. Reach is a benefit, not the concern.

Correct. Because contributions come from a large group of unverified strangers, quality and accuracy vary, and fake or biased reviews are a genuine risk. Verification is the core concern with crowdsourced content.

After this lesson, you will be able to:
• Explain that material created on a computer is the intellectual property of its creator and is protected by copyright
• Describe how creators use licenses, including Creative Commons and open source, to grant others permission to use their work under stated conditions
• Explain why using another person's work requires following its license and giving attribution, and why taking credit for it is plagiarism
• Identify material in the public domain and explain why downloading or distributing copyrighted work without permission can be illegal
• Apply legal and ethical reasoning to decide when a use needs permission, attribution, or neither

📈 Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 21 to 26 percent of the AP CSP exam, and legal and ethical questions about copyright, licensing, and attribution show up on nearly every practice test. The same rules govern the Create Performance Task, where you must cite any code or media you did not create, so this lesson protects both your score and your submission.

You find a perfect photo for your app with a quick image search, and you find a chunk of code on a public forum that does exactly what you need. Both are sitting right there on the open Internet, free to view. Does the fact that you can see and download something mean you are allowed to use it in your own project, and how would you even know?
You Made It, You Own It: Intellectual Property

When you create something original on a computer, a drawing, a song, a photo, a paragraph, or a program, that material is your intellectual property. It belongs to you as its creator. The moment an original creative work is fixed in a usable form, copyright automatically protects it. You do not have to register it or add a symbol for copyright to apply. Copyright gives the owner control over how the work is used, including who may copy it, share it, or build on it.

The flip side is the part students forget: other people's work is also their intellectual property. A photo you find online, a song clip, a block of code on a forum, all of it was created by someone who owns the copyright by default. Being able to see or download a work does not transfer any rights to you. Using it in your own project without permission can violate the owner's rights and can be illegal.

When a question involves reusing someone else's photo, music, or code, the exam wants you to check the license and give attribution, not to assume the work is free. The strongest answers respect the creator's ownership and follow the stated conditions for use.

Copyright would make sharing impossible if there were no way to grant permission, so creators use licenses. A license is the creator saying, in advance, ""you may use my work if you follow these conditions."" Two license systems appear constantly on the exam:

• A Creative Commons license lets a creator keep copyright while allowing others to use the work under stated conditions, such as giving attribution, using it only for non-commercial purposes, or releasing any changes under the same share-alike terms.

• An open source license applies to software and lets others use, modify, and share the source code under its conditions. Open source is about the freedom to read and change the code, not simply that the program is free of cost.
A license does not mean ""anything goes."" If a Creative Commons image requires attribution, you must credit the creator
column2: if it is non-commercial, you cannot use it to make money. Ignoring a condition means you are using the work outside its license, which puts you back to using it without permission.
only the owner may copy, share, or build on it unless they grant permission.

column1: Reuse of a copyrighted work under conditions the creator chooses, such as attribution, non-commercial, or share-alike.
Freedom to use, modify, and share software source code under the license's stated conditions.
No copyright applies, so the work is free for anyone to use for any purpose without permission.

A developer wants to include a background song and legally change it and re-share it, along with the underlying files, as long as they follow the stated conditions. Which permission is the developer looking for?

Nearly every license that lets you reuse a work asks for one thing in return: attribution, meaning you credit the original creator. Attribution is both a legal condition and an ethical duty. When you present someone else's work as your own, whether it is a paragraph, an image, or a block of code, that is plagiarism. Plagiarism is an ethical violation even when you technically had permission to use the work, because the wrong is claiming credit you did not earn.

Some material carries no copyright at all and sits in the public domain. This includes works whose copyright has expired and works released to the public deliberately. Public domain material is genuinely free to use for any purpose without permission, though crediting the source is still good practice and honest. Knowing whether something is public domain, licensed, or fully copyrighted is the difference between a legal reuse and an illegal one.

""It is on the Internet, so it is free to use."" This is false. Most content online is copyrighted the instant it is created, and being publicly visible grants you no rights at all. Downloading or distributing a copyrighted work without permission can be illegal. You must find the license, follow its conditions, and give attribution, or confirm the work is in the public domain, before you reuse it.

How This Shows Up on the Create Performance Task and the Exam

The Create Performance Task requires you to acknowledge and cite any code or media you did not create yourself. If you borrow a code segment from a library, a tutorial, or a classmate, or use an image, sound, or font made by someone else, you must credit the source in your program or written responses. 📈 Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 21 to 26 percent of the AP CSP exam, and safe computing questions on PII, phishing, authentication, and encryption are dependable points. The vocabulary is precise and testable, so a little memorization here converts directly into correct answers.

You get a text that looks like it is from your bank: it warns your account is locked and gives a link to 'verify your identity' by entering your password and Social Security number right now. The logo looks real and the message sounds urgent. Before you tap anything, what is the single biggest clue that this message might be a trap, and what should you do instead?

Personally identifiable information (PII) is information that can be used to identify a specific individual, either on its own or combined with other data. Examples include your full name, home address, government identification number, phone number, email address, date of birth, biometric data such as a fingerprint or face scan, and your physical location.

The core risk is simple: once information is online, it is very hard to remove and easy to copy. PII that gets exposed can be exploited for identity theft, used to track your movements and habits, or combined with other leaked data to launch targeted attacks. Even seemingly harmless details can be pieced together. Sharing less PII, and thinking before you post, reduces how much of you is exposed.

When a question asks about the danger of sharing PII, the strongest answer names a concrete harm such as identity theft, tracking, or targeted attacks, and recognizes that information online is hard to remove and easy to copy. Answers about convenience or speed are distractors.
Most attacks on ordinary users do not break encryption. They trick the user.

Phishing is a fraudulent message, often an email or text, designed to trick you into revealing credentials or PII, or into clicking a malicious link. Phishing usually creates urgency (""act now or lose access""), impersonates a trusted source, and sends you to a fake page that harvests what you type.
Malware is malicious software, such as a virus, that is installed without your informed consent to damage a system, steal data, or take control of a device.
Social engineering is the broad category of manipulating people into giving up information or access. Phishing is one kind of social engineering.

The common thread is that the human is the target. Signs of phishing include unexpected requests for a password or PII, links whose real address does not match the sender, pressure to act immediately, and small errors in the sender address or spelling.
Which of these is the clearest sign that an email is a phishing attempt?

Your first defense is a strong, unique password: long, hard to guess, and different for every account so that one breach does not unlock the rest. But passwords alone can be stolen or phished, which is why the strongest protection adds more factors.
Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires proof from two or more different kinds of factors before granting access. The three categories are:
Phone receiving a code, or a security key

The power of MFA is that an attacker who phishes your password still cannot log in without the second factor, such as the code on your phone. Other everyday protections include being cautious with links and app permissions, and keeping software updated so known vulnerabilities are patched.

Requiring two passwords, or a password plus a security question, is NOT multifactor authentication. Both are ""something you know,"" so they are the same kind of factor. True multifactor combines different kinds of factors, such as a password (know) plus a code from your phone (have).
Encryption encodes data so that only authorized parties can read it. The scrambled data means nothing to an eavesdropper without the correct key. There are two schemes you must distinguish:
A pair: a public key and a private key
The same key both encrypts and decrypts

column2: only the matching private key decrypts

column1: The key advantage of public key encryption is that two people who have never met can communicate securely. You publish your public key for anyone to use to encrypt a message to you, but you keep your private key secret, and only it can decrypt those messages.
